hook.support: Your boss says breaks are only for full-timers. Is that true? You have rights at work. You also have jobs to do. The facts are written down. You just need to know where.
hook.core: Your manager says casuals don’t get breaks, payslips are “a hassle”, and you’ll be paid for your trial “if it works out”. Is any of that legal? You have rights at work, and responsibilities too. The facts are written down by the people who make and enforce the rules. You just need to know where to look, and who to ask.
hook.extend: Every worker in Australia has rights and responsibilities. They are set out in official texts written for new workers. Learn to read those texts. Ask who they are for and what they are for. Then learn where to get reliable help. It is your best protection against being underpaid or unsafe.

why.support: Young workers are often paid the wrong amount. Knowing your rights helps you stop that.
why.core: Young workers are among the most likely to be underpaid or put at risk. Knowing your rights, and your responsibilities, means you can spot problems and get them fixed.
why.extend: Rights only protect you if you know them. Read official texts with care. Know which agency handles which problem. That turns rules on paper into real protection.

articles.title: Know what you’re owed

body.support:
Everyone at work has **rights** and **responsibilities**.

**Your rights include:**
- the right pay for your job and age.
- a **payslip** every time you’re paid.
- breaks.
- a safe place to work.
- being treated fairly.

**Your responsibilities include:**
- turning up on time.
- following safe instructions.
- working safely.
- telling someone if you see a danger.

When you start a job, your boss must give you a **Fair Work Information Statement**. It lists your main rights.

**Where to get help:**
- Pay problems: the **Fair Work Ombudsman**.
- Safety problems: **WorkSafe Victoria**.
- Advice: a union, or the **Young Workers Centre**.

These services are free.
body.core:
Every worker in Australia has **rights** (what you must get) and **responsibilities** (what you must do).

**Your rights include:**
- the minimum pay for your job and age, set by an **award**.
- a **payslip** within one working day of being paid.
- breaks and leave (casuals get a higher hourly rate instead of paid leave).
- a safe workplace, with training and safety gear.
- fair treatment, with no bullying.
- joining a union if you want to.

**Your responsibilities include:**
- turning up on time and doing the job.
- following reasonable and safe instructions.
- working safely, and reporting hazards.
- giving notice if you leave.

When you start, your employer must give you the **Fair Work Information Statement**. Casuals also get the **Casual Employment Information Statement**. These are official texts for new workers. They use plain words. Headings help you find what you need.

**Where to get help (all free):**
- Pay, breaks or conditions: the **Fair Work Ombudsman**.
- Safety: **WorkSafe Victoria**.
- **Wage theft** (when a boss underpays on purpose): the **Wage Inspectorate Victoria**.
- Advice and support: your union, or the **Young Workers Centre**.
body.extend:
Australian workers have legal **rights** and **responsibilities**. They come from laws, awards and agreements. Official texts explain them to workers.

**Core rights include:**
- minimum pay for your role and age, set by an **award**.
- a **payslip** within one working day of pay day.
- limits on weekly hours, and paid leave (casuals get a higher rate instead).
- a safe workplace, with training, supervision and safety gear.
- protection from bullying, discrimination and unfair sacking.
- the freedom to join a union.

**Responsibilities include:** following fair and lawful directions, working safely, reporting hazards and giving notice.

New employees must get the **Fair Work Information Statement**. Casuals also get the **Casual Employment Information Statement**. Their purpose is to inform. Their audience is new workers with no legal training. That shapes their features: plain words, short sections, headings and contact details.

**Reliable help depends on the problem:**
- pay and conditions: the **Fair Work Ombudsman**.
- health and safety: **WorkSafe Victoria**.
- **wage theft**, a crime in Victoria since 2021: the **Wage Inspectorate Victoria**.
- independent advice: unions and the **Young Workers Centre**.

Be wary of advice on forums or social media. Official sources are current and accurate.

caseStudies.title: When underpaying became a crime

body.support:
In **2021**, Victoria made a new law. If a boss **deliberately** underpays workers, it is a **crime**. It is called **wage theft**.

A boss can go to jail for up to **10 years**. A company can be fined over **$1 million**.

In **2022**, the Wage Inspectorate Victoria charged a restaurant in Macedon, and its owner. They were the first business in Australia to face these charges.

The charges said four former workers were not paid about **$7,000**. That included pay, extra weekend pay and super.

If you think you’re underpaid, you can get help. It’s free.
body.core:
On **1 July 2021**, Victoria became the first state to make deliberate underpayment of workers a **crime**. It’s called **wage theft**. Under the law, individuals can be jailed for up to **10 years**, and companies fined more than **$1.1 million**.

The law is enforced by the **Wage Inspectorate Victoria**.

In **2022**, the Inspectorate laid the first criminal wage theft charges in Australia. It charged a restaurant in Macedon, and its owner, with **94** offences. The charges alleged that four former staff were not paid about **$7,000** in wages, penalty rates and superannuation.

Many underpaid workers are young and in casual jobs. They often don’t know their rights, or are scared to speak up. The law gives them another place to go for help.
body.extend:
On **1 July 2021**, Victoria became the first state to make deliberate underpayment a crime: **wage theft**. A person can face up to **10 years’ jail**. A company can be fined more than **$1.1 million**. The **Wage Inspectorate Victoria** enforces the law.

In **2022**, the Inspectorate laid Australia’s first criminal wage theft charges. It charged a Macedon restaurant and its owner with **94** offences. It alleged that four former staff were short-changed about **$7,000**. That included wages, penalty rates and super.

The Fair Work system mostly gets money back through civil action. This law adds a criminal path. It targets underpaying on purpose, not honest mistakes.

Young casuals are often most at risk. They may not know their award or get payslips. They may fear losing shifts if they speak up. Knowing which agency handles which problem is the first step to a fix.

The case study is Victoria’s 2021 wage theft law and Australia’s first criminal wage theft charges (2022).

teacher.answers:
**Annotation:** 1 audience statement; 2 heading plus a right expressed with “must”; 3 precise, checkable detail (time limit); 4 brief summary of standards; 5 permission/choice (“can”); 6 contact details for help.

**Sort:** payslip — right (FWO); safety boots — responsibility; award rate — right (FWO); reporting a spill — responsibility; machine guard — right (WorkSafe); giving notice — responsibility.

**Case study:** from 1 July 2021, deliberate underpayment became a crime (up to 10 years’ jail, fines over $1.1m for companies); in 2022 a Macedon restaurant and owner faced 94 charges over about $7,000 allegedly owed to four former staff; young casuals often don’t know their award, lack payslips or fear losing shifts.

realityCheck: **Some students are being underpaid right now.** Expect disclosures. Point them to the Fair Work Ombudsman or the Young Workers Centre rather than advising on their case.
**Pay rules change.** Check payslip, award and leave details on fairwork.gov.au each year.
**Avoid naming the employer in the case study as guilty.** The source reports charges; the course says “charged” and “alleged”.
**Unions can be a political topic.** Present joining a union as a legal right and a source of advice, not as a recommendation.
**Works in a real class:** yes. Students with jobs immediately check their own payslips.
